elements.texte:
[cheerful] NutriBoost is hosting a private evening for its Paris customers.

The team wants to create a guests table to gather all the guests in it and send them their invitation.

Their first name, last name and email are in the customers table.

No need to copy them by hand: a query can fill the table automatically.
elements.avant: Store a query’s result in a table, new or already created.
elements.apres: CREATE TABLE guests creates a new table called guests.
phrases: NutriBoost is hosting a private evening for its Paris customers.
The team wants to create a guests table to gather all the guests in it and send them their invitation.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] CREATE TABLE guests creates a new table called guests.

After as, the select chooses the columns and rows to copy.

Here, the customers whose city is Paris.

The guests table gets 3 columns and 4 rows, one per Paris customer.

Its columns take the names from the select: first underscore name, last underscore name and email.

The table now exists in the database.
elements.avant: No need to copy them by hand: a query can fill the table automatically.
elements.apres: A week later, the evening is also opened to customers in Lyon.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] A week later, the evening is also opened to customers in Lyon.

The table already exists: we don’t create it again.

Insert into guests, followed by a select, adds the result’s rows.

The select reads the customers in Lyon: Lucas Bernard and Hugo Laurent.

The guests table goes from 4 to 6 rows.

Hugo Laurent has no email: his row comes in with null.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] Careful: the guests table has 3 columns.

Here, the select only provides two of them.

The query is rejected: 3 columns, but 2 values.

You need the same columns, in the same order as the table.

Otherwise, an email could end up in the last name column.
